findings.passage: Well, primarily, the law was not needed. We went from one of the better states exercising voter rights to one of the most restrictive. We have not one instance in 12 years - and that was a study done by the previous Secretary of State Cathy Cox - not one instance of voter fraud at the polls.
findings.note: NPR interview, as chair of the Georgia Legislative Black Caucus, on why the caucus opposed the 2005 Georgia photo ID law (SB 84). He says the law was not needed and cites no cases of in-person voter fraud.

findings.passage: No. There's definite evidence. I don't know where some of the other facts are found, but I know that 36 percent of senior citizens over 75 years old don't have driver's license and many forms of this identification the secretary of state talks about. Most of the fraud that occurs with voting is with absentee ballots, where only a signature is required. But none of these provisions will even addressed in Senate Bill 84. This is why many feel limiting voter fraud and securing our elections is not the motive with this SB 84 but instead who votes.
findings.note: Same NPR interview. He says many older people lack accepted photo ID, says absentee ballots need only a signature and SB 84 does not address them, and questions the motive for the bill.

findings.passage: And it directly affects black people and older folk who traditionally vote Democrat. This was a Republican game to lower the turnout - case closed.
findings.note: Same NPR interview. He says the photo ID law affects Black and older voters and says the aim was to lower turnout. Quoted exactly as spoken.
